In MDTs, people work together as equals to deliver a shared goal. If people feel more loyal to their professional background than to the team, they may make decisions that suit their profession rather than the project.
Set expectations early by agreeing how you’ll make decisions and set boundaries for each role, so everyone understands:
their role within the team
when they can decide alone
when they need to work together
shared responsibilities and collective decision making
Read the Service Manual guidance on governance principles for agile.

heading: Sharing working preferences
headingPath: Equal roles and decision making > Sharing working preferences
text:
It can be helpful if each team member shares a ‘manual of me’ – a short document setting out how they work best. It can cover:
work patterns and hours
communication preferences
skills
interests
When someone new joins, update these documents and run a ways of working session. Use this session to agree meeting schedules and frequencies, communication tools and decision-making processes.

heading: Improving how you work together
headingPath: Equal roles and decision making > Improving how you work together
text: Run retrospectives regularly to surface tensions, review your ways of working and fix issues quickly. Read the guidance on running retrospectives.

heading: Mapping stakeholders
headingPath: Equal roles and decision making > Mapping stakeholders
text:
Identify the people whose support, guidance or authority you need. You can map your stakeholders using the Team Onion framework by Emily Webber.
Think about who to involve, including:
the main MDT delivering the work
experts who advise the team, share contacts and inform decisions
senior stakeholders who support or champion the work and are part of your governance structure

heading: Including other organisations in your team
headingPath: Including other organisations in your team
text: Working across different organisations brings a wider range of experience and knowledge to a project. However, these teams can be more complex to set up and manage.

heading: Deciding who to involve
headingPath: Including other organisations in your team > Deciding who to involve
text:
The organisations you involve in your work will depend on your context. You may need insight from:
academia – to find out what research is happening in your area and who is doing it
the private sector – to understand how businesses work or for public-private partnerships
central government – if your work touches complex policy, ministerial priorities or related programmes
frontline staff – to understand how services work for the people you’re trying to reach
people with lived experience – if your work affects people in vulnerable situations or involves under-represented groups
local government – to understand context, what local leaders want and what’s happening nearby
voluntary, community and social enterprises – if these organisations play a big part in your area
You can bring people in on secondment or through informal arrangements. Secondments take longer to set up but are more secure. Informal arrangements are quicker but carry the risk of people being pulled away by other priorities. Be pragmatic about which route you use.

heading: Agreeing hosting and governance
headingPath: Including other organisations in your team > Agreeing hosting and governance
text:
Agree who hosts the team early. The host organisation usually sets the rules for:
what data you can access
what software and tools you use
where information is stored
which professional standards you follow
Governance must work across all the organisations involved. Oversight needs to stay flexible and proportionate.
Read the Service Manual guidance on governance principles for agile.

heading: Protecting the conditions you need to do the work
headingPath: Including other organisations in your team > Protecting the conditions you need to do the work
text: Each organisation you work with needs to give people time to do the work. Core team members need 15 hours or more a week on a test and learn project. Agree how daily tasks will be covered if they’re needed for urgent work in their own organisation.

heading: Using evidence to inform decisions
headingPath: Using evidence to inform decisions
text:
Use evidence to guide decision-making in every phase of the test and learn process. It can:
reduce bias
show where your assumptions are right or wrong
reduce risk by drawing on what’s already known
highlight uncertainty by revealing what’s not known
show what does and does not work
strengthen your rationale for what to do next
By combining different types of evidence, you can build a clearer, more convincing case for the choices you need to make.

heading: Using evidence to test assumptions
headingPath: Using evidence to inform decisions > Using evidence to test assumptions
text:
An assumption is something you believe but have not proved with evidence. The test and learn process relies on teams identifying and validating assumptions.
The process runs in a cycle:
Use evidence to identify assumptions.
Test these assumptions by gathering more evidence.
Make decisions based on the evidence, which will raise new assumptions to test.
Keep repeating this cycle as you move towards your outcome, using learnings to update your theory of change.
Read the guidance on creating a testing plan.

heading: Ways to gather evidence
headingPath: Ways to gather evidence
text:
You can collect evidence by:
reviewing existing evidence
talking to people with lived experience
talking to subject matter experts
conducting structured research
Each evidence type helps you build a case for your decisions and agree on what to do next. Use your findings to explain the reasoning behind your choices.
Before you start, you can read the Nesta practice guide on using research evidence.

heading: Reviewing existing evidence
headingPath: Ways to gather evidence > Reviewing existing evidence
text:
Look at existing evidence in the early phases of test and learn to understand your challenge area.
Review ideas tested in different fields and think about how to apply them to your work. For example, you can learn about:
running safety checks from air travel
streamlining repeatable tasks from the fast food industry
keeping users engaged from video games
Existing evidence gives you a framework for decision making. It cannot prove what will work for you because every situation is different. If you rely too much on what other people have done in different contexts, you risk making false comparisons.
Use existing evidence to:
learn what has worked well elsewhere
learn from mistakes made elsewhere
create a logical framework for your assumptions
think about your challenge area from a different angle
find innovative ideas from different fields
You can then use these insights to form assumptions, for example an approach:
worked in a similar context, so it might work for your challenge area
improved outcomes in a different challenge area, so you should explore if it’ll work for you

heading: Talking to people with lived experience
headingPath: Ways to gather evidence > Talking to people with lived experience
text:
Talk early and often to the people affected by issues in your challenge area. Their insights will help you design interventions that meet their needs.
Structured research is the main way to talk to people with lived experience. People may also share stories with you informally. Listen to them with empathy and respect, but do not treat informal conversations as research data. One person’s experience may be typical or unusual. You need to do structured research to find that out. If you rely too much on evidence from a small number of people, you risk designing interventions that only work for a minority.
Talk to people with lived experience to:
identify friction and frustrations
understand possible motivations for behaviour
raise assumptions that you can test later
collect stories and quotes to help explain an issue
Use these insights to form assumptions to test. For example if someone finds a step in a service frustrating, you can assume other users may also drop out at that point. Or if someone says an incentive motivated them, you should check whether that incentive has been used elsewhere.

heading: Talking to subject matter experts
headingPath: Ways to gather evidence > Talking to subject matter experts
text:
Subject matter experts help you make sense of complex or technical problems. Even if you have experts in your team, no single person can tell you everything you need. Expert input reflects individual judgement and experience which may include personal biases, outdated knowledge or conflicts of interest. Always balance expert views with other evidence to avoid relying on authority or keeping things as they are.
Talk to experts to:
build trust and credibility with stakeholders
guide decisions in fields where your team’s expertise is limited
explore strategies and assumptions
understand technical findings through an expert lens
identify potential weaknesses in test ideas
Use these insights to form assumptions to test. For example, if an expert identifies a technical risk, you can design your test to reduce it. Or if frontline service staff report a bottleneck, you can test whether that process is contributing to delays.

heading: Conducting structured research
headingPath: Ways to gather evidence > Conducting structured research
text:
Structured research is when you collect data through a recognised research method, such as surveys, experiments or interviews. Unlike informal conversations, structured research is planned in advance and aims to produce repeatable results. If someone uses your method, they should find similar or comparable results.
You’re less likely to use structured research at the start of your test and learn work. You’re more likely to use it as you move through design and into testing.
Structured research helps you assess the extent of an issue and reduces bias. It collects 2 types of data:
quantitative data, which is numerical information that helps identify trends or show if an action causes a result
qualitative data, which provide insights into people’s experiences that explain why something is happening
Setting your scope can limit what you find. Be aware that you could miss findings outside your research area, lose important detail or narrow your focus too much. For example, relying too much on quantitative data could make you focus on changing numbers rather than meeting user needs.
You can use structured research to:
understand the size or frequency of what you’re interested in
identify trends and patterns
test assumptions generated by other forms of evidence
prove whether something is working
understand why something is or is not working
Turn these insights into assumptions to test. For example, if quantitative data shows that two-thirds of users experience a problem, you can assume this is a widespread issue you need to resolve. Or if qualitative data shows people struggle to access a service on mobile phones, you can assume this is why case numbers have dropped after a website relaunch.

heading: Combining different types of evidence
headingPath: Combining different types of evidence
text:
Use a range of evidence to support your decisions. There are 4 main types of evidence you can use:
analogical, to compare with a similar or related situation
anecdotal, to understand user stories and experiences
testimonial, to provide expert views and opinions
statistical, to show scale, measure impact and identify trends using numerical data
Using a mix of these evidence types helps build a clear and convincing rationale for decision making.
Test and learn teams are multidisciplinary, including people with a range of skills and perspectives. Each role uses distinct methods to gather evidence. For example, a user researcher and a data analyst will approach the same question from different angles and find out different things. Use the mixed methods research practice to combine your team’s qualitative and quantitative evidence, rather than relying on one person’s findings.

heading: Cross-checking results
headingPath: Combining different types of evidence > Cross-checking results
text:
Check your findings against different sources of evidence. For example, if you identify a trend in existing evidence, ask people affected by the issue if it matches their experience.
Finding the same pattern across sources gives you higher confidence in your results. This is known as triangulation.

heading: Filling gaps in your understanding
headingPath: Combining different types of evidence > Filling gaps in your understanding
text:
Use different types of evidence to explore different aspects of an issue. For example, if structured research shows a service feature is not working, talking to service users or experts could explain why.
Combining these insights gives you a broader understanding than one source would provide. This is known as complementarity.

heading: Bringing findings together
headingPath: Combining different types of evidence > Bringing findings together
text:
Bring your evidence together to get a clearer understanding of a problem, rather than keeping the sources separate. For example, you can use:
data about problems in one service to inform discussions with users of another
interview insights to design tools that collect numerical data
Combining your evidence leads to deeper insights. This is known as integration.

heading: Theory of change
headingPath: Theory of change
text:
A theory of change visually maps:
how your activities lead to the outcomes you want to achieve
the assumptions you’re making about how that change will happen
Developing a theory of change provides a foundation for your test and learn project, setting out the logic for:
how your intervention will work
what you should test along the way

heading: Benefits of using a theory of change
headingPath: Theory of change > Benefits of using a theory of change
text:
A theory of change helps you:
agree on what you want to achieve through testing
check that your activities, expected results and evidence are linked
identify and challenge your assumptions
spot unintended consequences
avoid solution-first thinking
Solution-first thinking happens when you choose an idea because you like it. Base your decisions on evidence that an idea will improve outcomes.
Draft a theory of change for your intervention once you know the outcomes you want to achieve.

heading: Creating a theory of change
headingPath: Theory of change > Creating a theory of change
text:
Involve stakeholders by running an online or in-person workshop. Working together helps to:
build shared understanding
invite constructive challenge
Start by listing the impact and outcomes you want to achieve. Then map out the activities and resources needed to reach them.
Use a draft that is partly filled in to help stakeholders who have:
limited time
different levels of knowledge
You do not have to finish your theory of change in one session. Developing it over time gives people a chance to reflect between sessions.
Before you start, you can read the Government Analysis Function theory of change toolkit.

heading: Iterating your theory of change
headingPath: Theory of change > Iterating your theory of change
text:
Your theory of change should be a living document.
As you move through the test and learn phases, you’ll learn more about how your intervention works. Update your theory of change regularly using evidence of what works and what does not. This process gives you a strong rationale for how each iteration supports your intended outcomes.

heading: Developing your research plan
headingPath: Developing your research plan
text:
For some projects, you’ll need to research sensitive topics or work with people in vulnerable situations. This research can cause distress if you do not plan carefully. You must know how to protect both participants and researchers.
Consider your approach to:
participant circumstances, such as experiencing homelessness, claiming benefits or experiencing abuse
participant characteristics, such as age, health condition or disability
community context, such as religious practices, cultural sensitivities or language needs
Anyone taking part in research sessions needs safeguarding training. Ask your safeguarding team to arrange training for anyone who needs it.
Look for existing research and personal accounts from the people or communities you’re designing for. Make every effort to use these sources before asking participants to take part.

heading: Getting expert input
headingPath: Developing your research plan > Getting expert input
text:
Involve a topic expert or someone from the community in your project. Ask for their input when creating your research plan and questions.
They can help you:
use appropriate language
find the right participants
understand how you may be seen as a researcher

heading: Assessing risks to participants
headingPath: Assessing risks to participants
text:
Identify any risks or harm your research could cause to participants, such as:
emotional or psychological harm
physical harm
financial loss
environmental or social impact

heading: Creating a safeguarding protocol
headingPath: Assessing risks to participants > Creating a safeguarding protocol
text:
You must create a protocol that sets out what to do if a participant discloses abuse, harm or neglect.
Get in touch with your safeguarding team and ask them to review your protocol.
If you cannot protect your participants, find a better method for your research.
For advice on keeping participants safe, read:
safeguarding if a participant tells you about abuse, harm or neglect
how to arrange support for participants
Department for Education guidance on participant safeguarding

heading: Completing an ethics assessment
headingPath: Completing an ethics assessment
text:
You must complete an ethics assessment showing your research is justified and your plan has clear objectives.
Your research may need formal ethical approval, for example, if there is a high risk of harm. If you think you might need approval, get advice before starting.

heading: Managing data
headingPath: Completing an ethics assessment > Managing data
text:
Your research may involve collecting personal information about participants. Ask your organisation’s Data Protection Officer how to store and anonymise research data safely.
You should complete a data protection impact assessment and, if needed, a data sharing agreement.
For help preparing these documents, read:
Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) guidance on data protection impact assessments
ICO guidance on data sharing agreements
You must be extra careful if your research includes sensitive information, such as health data or sexual orientation. This is called ‘special category data’.

heading: Recruiting participants
headingPath: Recruiting participants
text:
Make sure recruitment documents describe:
your research objectives
what will happen in the session
how you’ll use the participants’ information
Tell participants which sensitive topics you want to discuss. Let them know they do not need to answer every question.
Give participants a choice on how to take part, so they feel safe. Let them choose how, where and when the research happens.
Consider whether recording the session is appropriate for the topic. Always allow participants to opt out of being recorded.

heading: Asking for consent
headingPath: Recruiting participants > Asking for consent
text:
Your consent form must explain when you’ll need to share the participant’s information with others, including disclosures of:
unreported abuse
neglect
criminal activity
harm to themselves or others
If a participant is under 16 years old, you must get parental consent.
Read Department for Education guidance on how to gather and store informed consent.

heading: Running research sessions
headingPath: Running research sessions
text:
Consider arranging a call with participants before their session to:
introduce yourself
go over the consent form
explain your objectives with the research
discuss any support needs
The more you know about each participant, the more you can adjust the session to meet their needs.
To avoid delays in the session you could also check all technical equipment and software works.

heading: Arranging support for participants
headingPath: Running research sessions > Arranging support for participants
text:
Encourage participants to bring someone to the session to support them. This person will also need to sign a consent form – read about asking for consent.
Participants could also give you the name of someone they can call during the session and immediately after.
Prepare a list of contact details for relevant support organisations, charities or services that you can share with participants at the end of the session.

heading: During a session
headingPath: Running research sessions > During a session
text:
Always run research sessions in pairs when working with people in vulnerable situations. The observer should remain quiet and take notes. Their involvement protects the participant and ensures you have support.
You should:
use the language the participant uses to describe themselves or their situation
ask the participant to clarify if you do not understand something they say
acknowledge and validate the participant’s experiences
avoid offering advice
Let the participant:
tell their story in their own way
decide how much to share
skip questions they do not want to answer
If a participant becomes emotional ask if they would like to pause or continue. Remind them they can stop at any time and reassure them they’ll still receive any incentives you’ve offered.
At the end of the session, share information about relevant support services with the participant. Acknowledge that talking about physical or mental health can be difficult. Explain that you do this with all participants, in case they find it helpful.

heading: After a session
headingPath: Running research sessions > After a session
text:
You could send participants:
session notes, so they can remove anything they do not want included in the research
a summary of findings and next steps, to give a supportive end to their involvement
Run a debrief with the team after the session. Use this time to discuss anything difficult or to ask for more support.

heading: Safeguarding if a participant tells you about abuse, harm or neglect
headingPath: Running research sessions > Safeguarding if a participant tells you about abuse, harm or neglect
text:
Tell the participant you must share information about abuse, harm or neglect. Report the disclosure to your safeguarding team as soon as possible.
Record your questions and the participant’s answers as accurately as possible. Do not paraphrase or make assumptions. Write down the time and date of the disclosure. If you decide not to escalate the issue, write down the reason for your decision.
Keep the note private and stored securely.

heading: Looking after yourself as a researcher
headingPath: Looking after yourself as a researcher
text:
Create a wellbeing and support plan with your research team ahead of the sessions. Following a plan helps make sure you and your team are prepared for challenging topics.
Limit the number of sessions you schedule in a day. Taking regular breaks gives you time to:
recover between sessions
focus on each participant
stay alert to safeguarding concerns
You can also read the Justice Digital blog post on how to keep colleagues safe in research.

heading: What this phase is about
headingPath: What this phase is about
text:
In this phase you narrow a broad challenge area down to a starting point you can work with.
A main principle of test and learn is that it focuses on outcomes. It’s about the difference an intervention can make to people’s lives. This phase is about getting clear on what you want to achieve, before you start looking for solutions.
By the end of this phase, you should have agreed:
a high-level outcome measure
a problem statement that links to that measure and can guide test and learn activity

heading: Main aims of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Main aims of this phase
text:
The main aims of this phase are to:
understand the strategic context of the challenge area
narrow the challenge area down to a problem statement and outcomes
build consensus among the team, main partners and stakeholders
identify the big decisions you need to make and the deliverables your research will support
find opportunities for ideas to take into testing, for example from stakeholder engagement, desk research or data analysis
You may need to do some work before this phase to:
make the case for test and learn
create the conditions for test and learn

heading: Outcomes of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Outcomes of this phase
text:
At the end of this phase you should have:
a high-level understanding of the problem area, who is impacted and initiatives that currently exist
engaged main stakeholders, such as policymakers, service leaders, community organisations and think tanks
agreed which partners to involve in decision making, including on scope
agreed an overarching outcome to begin exploring test ideas

heading: Identifying the challenge area
headingPath: Identifying the challenge area
text:
A challenge area is the policy problem or systemic issue you want to improve.
You can apply test and learn principles to many policy and delivery challenges by researching user needs and getting early feedback.
But test and learn is most valuable when:
the stakes are high, or outcomes clearly need improving
there is little evidence about what works
you do not know how residents will react to or use a service
you can measure outcomes or proxy outcomes quickly
there is a realistic way to scale what works
For example, there are many practical delivery questions that come with a shift to neighbourhood-centred healthcare. How do you identify people earlier? How do you organise partners around neighbourhoods? How do you use data safely?
Test and learn methods can help you build early evidence of what works before changing whole systems.

heading: Narrowing down the challenge
headingPath: Identifying the challenge area > Narrowing down the challenge
text:
Your challenge area may be broad to begin with. Use research and work with your partners to:
agree on a more tightly defined outcome measure and problem statement
set boundaries for test and learn
These agreements should be specific enough to begin to identify opportunities for testing.
As your focus narrows, it’s important to build:
a clear rationale for how the problem links to the overarching outcome
support and agreement among decision makers and team members
This phase is rarely linear. In practice, the scope may narrow and then widen again as you learn more.

heading: Example: creating a problem statement
headingPath: Identifying the challenge area > Narrowing down the challenge > Example: creating a problem statement
text:
Challenge area: helping young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) aged 16 and over move from school into further education, training or work.
Overarching outcome: reduce the number of young people with SEND who are not in education, employment or training (NEET).
Problem statement: how can we identify young people with SEND who are most at risk of becoming NEET and offer them support?

heading: Choosing which challenge to improve
headingPath: Choosing which challenge to improve
text:
Use evidence from different sources to narrow down the challenge area. You may find several problems that could be a good fit for test and learn. Be led by:
a clear overarching outcome
stakeholder priorities
energy and momentum
Throughout this phase, you can build a backlog of problems to revisit later.
Questions to explore:
Why are services not delivering the intended outcomes?
What has already been tried and what works?
What initiatives are running and where is there momentum?
What does local data show about service gaps or specific user groups?

heading: Desk research and policy analysis
headingPath: Choosing which challenge to improve > Desk research and policy analysis
text:
Review strategies, white papers, data and research to understand:
the ambition and commitments made, including targets, outcomes or delivery priorities
existing initiatives, mapping current services to identify gaps and avoid duplication
the gap between current and desired states, and where doing things differently could make an impact
urgent priorities, including milestones or deliverables suited to a test and learn approach
Read guidance on reviewing existing evidence.

heading: Stakeholder engagement
headingPath: Choosing which challenge to improve > Stakeholder engagement
text:
Relationship building is an important part of test and learn. Create a stakeholder map and engage stakeholders to:
understand the challenge through different perspectives
build collective commitment to prioritising the problem
identify who needs to make final decisions on scope – aim for the simplest governance model

heading: User research
headingPath: Choosing which challenge to improve > User research
text:
Explore real-life experiences of the challenge area through user research to:
understand the main issues facing those affected
see how services work from the user’s perspective
create problem statements that reflect experiences of the main user groups

heading: Analysis
headingPath: Choosing which challenge to improve > Analysis
text:
Explore existing research and evaluation in your challenge area to:
see what evidence says about how to achieve your intended outcomes
review local, national and international efforts in the area
create a log of ideas that have been tested elsewhere
Explore existing data in your challenge area to:
find measures and data for your intended outcomes
build an understanding of the issue by analysing public and internal datasets
identify specific groups of people you could test with
check what data is held locally, and make sure it’s linked and ready for when you need it
check what data is held nationally or by others, such as charities, universities and businesses, so you can plan for sharing it later

heading: Agreeing on your focus
headingPath: Choosing which challenge to improve > Agreeing on your focus
text:
In complex challenge areas there will be various opportunities for test and learn. You will need to balance the desire to learn more about a challenge with the necessity of agreeing on a narrower scope.
Your timings and approach will depend on your local context. For example, relationships, organisational priorities and ownership of the challenge will influence how quickly you progress.
You can help build momentum and move the work forward by recommending opportunities that are backed by evidence-based rationale.

heading: Example: defining the challenge in your local context
headingPath: Choosing which challenge to improve > Example: defining the challenge in your local context
text:
Early in the Test, Learn and Grow (TLG) programme, demonstrator teams were set up to prove the concept. They ran 12-week projects in partnership with central and local government, showing how to put the approach into practice. Teams had to agree quickly, both on the challenge area and the focus for test and learn, prioritising speed over depth.
At a later stage of TLG, accelerator teams had different priorities. They were tasked with specific challenge areas, such as economic inactivity or violence against women and girls. These areas represent significant national challenges and are priorities for both central and local government.
These teams spent 3 to 6 months narrowing the challenges into test and learn opportunities.
They focused on:
building relationships with local partners
looking at challenge areas from different perspectives
understanding local contexts
getting support for the test and learn approach

heading: What this phase is about
headingPath: What this phase is about
text: In this phase you use research to explore opportunities for testing. The aim is to use evidence to develop a shortlist of test ideas that relate to the problem statement.

heading: Main aims of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Main aims of this phase
text:
The main aims of this phase are to:
use evidence to further scope the challenge area and problem statement
identify where and how doing things differently might improve outcomes
explore and understand how people with lived experience are affected by the issue
develop and prioritise test ideas to design

heading: Outcomes of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Outcomes of this phase
text:
At the end of this phase you should have:
a deeper understanding of issues and opportunities relating to the problem statement
a shortlist of test ideas
a theory of change
agreement from partners or decision makers on test ideas to design

heading: Related guidance
headingPath: What this phase is about > Related guidance
text:
Before starting this phase you can:
read the Service Manual guidance on user research
read the Department for Education user research manual
take the FutureLearn course on user research in government

heading: Planning your approach to scoping
headingPath: Planning your approach to scoping
text:
How you approach scoping depends on your situation. You may be exploring the idea of a new service or intervention, or considering how to adapt something that already exists.
Scoping takes time. Consider:
local context
availability of existing data and findings
access to local people and staff
Balance ambition with pragmatism. That means setting a bold, transformative vision while defining a focused, deliverable starting point. Prioritising helps you manage this balance without choosing a solution too early.
Work with local partners to turn opportunities into manageable test ideas. Involve your team and stakeholders in the research of your ideas. This helps people new to test and learn see how user insight and evidence guide each phase.

heading: What you need to find out
headingPath: Planning your approach to scoping > What you need to find out
text:
The amount of research you do in this phase depends on the evidence you already have.
If you’re starting with a clearly defined local problem, you may need less initial research. Before you move to design, make sure you validate the problem with community groups and people with lived experience.
If you’re working with a broad or less defined opportunity, use research in this phase to understand:
how existing services are working for users
the context of the challenge area and the wider system
local context, such as cultural practices in the community
what frontline staff think are the main problems in the service and system
what is already happening locally to address the problem
assumptions people have about the problem and opportunities to solve it

heading: Example: building an understanding of local context
headingPath: Planning your approach to scoping > What you need to find out > Example: building an understanding of local context
text:
The Test, Learn and Grow team and Northumberland County Council wanted to find out how Family Hub services could work more closely with schools and early years providers. This work aimed to help more reception-age children meet early learning goals.
Because effective early intervention relies on strong local networks, the team started by researching existing connections in Northumberland.
They wanted to understand:
how schools, early years providers and Family Hubs worked together
which families were using local services and which missed out
what it felt like for families and staff to use these services
how to measure the effectiveness of building stronger connections
The team ran 38 interviews with staff and families. They spoke to local authority staff, Hub managers and staff from schools and early years providers, both those working with the Hubs and not. And they spent time listening to parents, speaking to regular Family Hubs users and those who had never visited.
They then combined interview insights with quantitative analysis and desk research.
These activities helped the team:
understand local services, relationships and parents’ experiences
narrow their scope to 5 opportunity areas
build trust and ongoing local partnerships

heading: Researching with staff and communities
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities
text:
Involve local people and communities from the start of your project. Use research and participatory design methods to understand the opportunity from a local perspective.
Policymakers and people with lived experience often see issues differently.

heading: Ways to gather insights
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities > Ways to gather insights
text:
Start by reviewing existing local research.
If you need to gather more insights you could use:
focus groups to discuss local problems
workshops with participatory activities, for example systems mapping or design probes
shadowing and ethnographic research to observe and understand how things work in real life
interviews to hear the experiences of local people

heading: Identifying who to speak to
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities > Identifying who to speak to
text:
You should write research questions and make a research plan. Use these to help you identify who you need to speak to, including:
frontline staff
people working locally or across the challenge area, for example in voluntary organisations or community groups
people with lived experience

heading: Ethics and safety
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities > Ethics and safety
text:
You must make sure you conduct your research safely and sensitively, especially if you’re working with people in vulnerable situations.
Before you start, read about:
conducting research safely
inclusive design in the Service Manual
participatory design
ethical principles in the Ministry of Justice Design System

heading: Systems mapping
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities > Systems mapping
text:
Creating a systems map is a good way to start exploring an opportunity. It looks beyond a service to include everything that can influence or change a system.
Mapping helps you identify:
work already underway in the challenge area
people and organisations you need to speak to and where they connect
areas of friction and things that are working well
opportunities for further research
Use the process to develop a shared understanding of the system in your team and with partners. Share the map with subject matter experts and stakeholders to check your findings and add to it.
Update the map as you learn and the system becomes clearer, or changes.
Get started with the systems thinking toolkit for civil servants.

heading: Example: mapping Children’s Services to improve support
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities > Systems mapping > Example: mapping Children’s Services to improve support
text:
The Test, Learn and Grow team worked with Barnsley Council to map processes in Children’s Services and speak to social workers about their day-to-day experiences. This work supported efforts to see how AI and data tools could help improve outcomes for children in care.
The team began by looking at the Council’s case management system, gathering detailed information about technology, workflows and legal requirements.
As trust grew, staff shared experiences of working in Children’s Services, including stories of families they tried to help and the obstacles they encountered. These conversations gave the team insight into social workers’ daily activities and the challenges families and staff face.
This work revealed a gap. While the map showed formal processes, it did not show where there were opportunities for earlier intervention. The team decided to test whether council data could track how children move through services, so they could provide targeted help earlier.

heading: Design probes
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities > Design probes
text: Use design probes, also called cultural probes, to engage local people in your research and design. Participants interact with carefully chosen objects, documents or tasks to generate insights and new ideas. You can run design probes individually or in workshops.

heading: Example: using design probes to identify what problem to focus on
headingPath: Researching with staff and communities > Design probes > Example: using design probes to identify what problem to focus on
text:
The Test, Learn and Grow team worked with Islington Council to develop test ideas that would help tackle violence against women and girls.
They held a workshop with local survivors, using a tree metaphor as a design probe to break down each idea and assess how it would work in practice.
The group used the metaphor to consider:
roots – the foundations and conditions needed
trunk – who is involved and responsible
leaves – the benefits and outcomes
bird’s-eye view – how the idea fits into the wider system
This exercise helped the team identify which parts of each idea they could explore further in testing.

heading: Analysing data
headingPath: Analysing data
text:
Combine data and user research to understand the problem and validate findings.
The data you use will depend on what is available and the level of detail you need. You could look at:
national data, to compare local trends with national averages
local demographic or deprivation data, to identify where you want to focus your work
service data, such as agency usage statistics, user journeys through the service, helpdesk logs, website analytics or annual reports

heading: Example: using data to see the journeys people take through services
headingPath: Analysing data > Example: using data to see the journeys people take through services
text:
The Test, Learn and Grow team worked with data analysts from Islington Council Children’s Services to understand:
how domestic abuse cases move through Children’s Services
how many cases are turned away because they do not meet the services’ eligibility criteria
The team used this data to develop their understanding of the problem and identify opportunities for interventions.

heading: Analysing research and refining the scope
headingPath: Analysing research and refining the scope
text: Document and review your findings as you work to narrow your focus. Create a theory of change as you plan for the next phase.

heading: Documenting research
headingPath: Analysing research and refining the scope > Documenting research
text:
Record your research while it’s fresh in your mind to help you capture accurate insight and share evidence with stakeholders.
You could create:
a systems map
a user journey map
a user needs log
an insights log
an evidence review
an assumptions log

heading: Analysing and synthesising research
headingPath: Analysing research and refining the scope > Analysing and synthesising research
text:
You should analyse your research continually. Read the Service Manual guidance on how to analyse a research session.
You have enough information and evidence to move to the next phase when you have:
summarised clear themes
defined the problem within your local context
narrowed down the test ideas for design in the next phase
created a theory of change to map how your ideas will work
Use your findings to turn insights into actions for the next phase. You could create:
opportunity areas by using idea cards or storyboards to define test ideas and show how research insights could help solve parts of the problem
problem statements by iterating your initial challenge using “How might we” questions, such as “How might we increase the positive influence of parents on children’s employment outcomes?”

heading: Prioritising ideas to test
headingPath: Prioritising ideas to test
text: Once you’ve explored your test ideas, you need to evaluate them and focus your effort.

heading: Setting criteria to refine your scope
headingPath: Prioritising ideas to test > Setting criteria to refine your scope
text:
Set your criteria based on:
research and evidence
outcomes
strategic priorities
Next, check your options against desirability, feasibility and viability.

heading: Desirability
headingPath: Prioritising ideas to test > Desirability
text:
To check if an idea is the right thing to work on, consider whether it:
delivers measurable benefits for local users, the community and staff
supports change across the wider system
aligns with your strategic priorities

heading: Feasibility
headingPath: Prioritising ideas to test > Feasibility
text:
To check if you can realistically do the design work now, consider whether you:
have the skills, experience and time in your team
have the technology and data you need
can gather evidence to track change and measure success
can involve local people in designing solutions, including groups that are less engaged

heading: Viability
headingPath: Prioritising ideas to test > Viability
text:
To check if the designed idea will be supported and sustained, consider:
senior buy-in, to make sure local and national leaders understand and back the work
team commitment to testing new approaches
scalability, so the work can expand over time, influence the wider system or be adapted by other teams

heading: Running a prioritisation workshop
headingPath: Prioritising ideas to test > Running a prioritisation workshop
text:
A prioritisation workshop will help you shortlist your test ideas. Involve stakeholders and the community or service users, if relevant.
Assess each test idea against basic requirements. Rule out any that do not fit.
Review the prioritisation criteria as a team. Add or remove criteria to fit your context.
Check the remaining test ideas against the criteria, and rank them low, medium or high.
Use dot voting to choose the idea you’ll start with, then agree your next steps.
The outcome should be a clear, agreed scope. Everyone in the team should understand what you’re working on and why.

heading: Example: using research and participatory design to prioritise ideas for testing
headingPath: Prioritising ideas to test > Example: using research and participatory design to prioritise ideas for testing
text:
In Wakefield, the Test, Learn and Grow team used participatory design and user research to narrow down test ideas for helping young people into employment.
The team worked with local partners following a 5-step process.
The team identified 24 opportunity areas through desk research, systems mapping and problem-framing workshops with council and voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) staff.
Council and VCSE staff voted on the most important challenges, narrowing these 24 opportunity areas down to 5.
The team combined their own research with an AI-assisted review of academic and policy research across the 5 opportunity areas. They created a map showing how young people move between education and employment.
The team ran user research with young people and employment staff, using questions from the mapping to guide discussions. The research produced 28 problem statements, which the team narrowed to 9 based on feasibility and desirability.
Council and VCSE staff voted to decide the top 3 opportunity areas, and together with the team developed test ideas for each one.

heading: What this phase is about
headingPath: What this phase is about
text:
In this phase you use participatory methods to develop test ideas into prototypes. You’ll work with relevant groups, including:
people with lived experience
local staff
voluntary, community or social enterprise partners

heading: Main aims of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Main aims of this phase
text:
The main aims of this phase are to:
involve service users and staff to ensure their insights and experiences shape the design
develop ideas into prototypes for testing

heading: Outcomes of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Outcomes of this phase
text:
At the end of this phase you should have:
designed ideas that meet user needs and support better outcomes
created at least one prototype for testing
identified what you’ll test first
iterated your theory of change

heading: Using participatory methods for design
headingPath: Using participatory methods for design
text:
In this phase, you’ll use participatory design to create a testable prototype alongside the people who will use or deliver the service.
When designing your prototype, you should involve:
people with lived experience of the issue
operational staff who work in government or voluntary, community or social enterprises (VCSEs)
Staff in VCSEs may work in services connected to the challenge area, or know people with lived experience. Include them when you:
decide what to prototype
design the prototype
Work with them as equal decision makers from the start, or create opportunities for feedback by running design workshops or show and tells.
Always make sure you conduct research safely and compensate members of the public for their time.

heading: Planning how to involve people in the work
headingPath: Using participatory methods for design > Planning how to involve people in the work
text:
It’s important to do participatory design carefully and sensitively. To make participation meaningful, consider:
who to work with
how to collaborate
when to bring people in to the process
To decide how much to involve people, check that you can:
give them influence over decisions and what you do next
keep them safe, especially when discussing sensitive topics
make taking part feel worthwhile, even for people with limited time
Do not work with participants if you cannot guarantee their safety.

heading: Consequence scanning and identifying risks of your idea
headingPath: Consequence scanning and identifying risks of your idea
text:
Assessing risk is especially important if you’re testing with people in vulnerable situations. You could run:
a consequence scanning workshop – read the Doteveryone guide to consequence scanning
a premortem – read the Atlassian guide to premortem project management strategy
These sessions help you to:
consider risks from the start
plan how to mitigate them during testing

heading: Example: using consequence scanning to identify risks in testing
headingPath: Consequence scanning and identifying risks of your idea > Example: using consequence scanning to identify risks in testing
text:
The Test Learn and Grow team worked with Islington Council to assess the possible effects of testing an idea to tackle violence against women and girls.
They ran a consequence scanning workshop to:
identify possible unintended risks as well as the positive impacts they hoped to achieve
create a log recording how they would reduce the risks
review risks and impacts with staff to discuss what was happening in practice and any changes they could make

heading: Creating a prototype
headingPath: Creating a prototype
text:
A prototype is a way of making your ideas real, so you can:
see how they work
reduce the risk in your decisions
get feedback
fix things that do not work before you start testing
Prototypes help you learn where and how to improve an idea. Read about the principles of prototyping to guide your approach.

heading: Prototyping with participatory design methods
headingPath: Creating a prototype > Prototyping with participatory design methods
text:
Use participatory design methods to create your first prototype with local people and partners. You could:
hold workshops to map out steps together and refine the design as you gather feedback
run focus groups or research sessions to test specific parts of your idea
test early prototypes with participants
Use the insights you gather from these sessions to update your theory of change so it reflects your latest understanding of how an intervention will work.

heading: Choosing what to prototype
headingPath: Creating a prototype > Choosing what to prototype
text:
Start with the questions you need to answer before you move into testing. These should form the focus of your prototype.
Next, decide on the smallest thing you can make to answer those questions, and choose the format that suits them best.
Sketch your idea before creating something more detailed to:
get early insights into what works
save time and effort

heading: Prototype formats
headingPath: Creating a prototype > Prototype formats
text:
A prototype could be a:
sketch
letter
poster
storyboard
service map or walkthrough
Wizard of Oz simulation, which mimics how a service or intervention would work - read the Interaction Design Foundation guide to Wizard of Oz prototypes
wireframe created with design software such as Miro or Figma
website built on a platform such as the GOV.UK Prototype Kit
For detailed methods of prototyping, explore section 07 Prototyping in the This is Service Design Doing method library.

heading: Prototyping approaches
headingPath: Creating a prototype > Prototyping approaches
text:
Depending on what you’re testing, you could use:
paper prototypes, such as sending a mock-up letter to households and asking for feedback
prototypes in code, such as building wireframes users can click through to test a new triage app
service prototypes, such as testing a proposed support programme with a sample group of parents to see if they find the options helpful

heading: Example: co-designing an early years intervention with local services
headingPath: Creating a prototype > Example: co-designing an early years intervention with local services
text:
In Manchester, the Test, Learn and Grow team interviewed council staff and parents to find ways to help more reception-age children meet early learning goals. The findings showed that joined-up services supported families better. Staff then wanted to see if Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) data could identify how services might reach children, before problems developed.
The team brought together frontline staff and senior leaders from across schools, early years providers, Family Hubs and the local authority. In 2 design workshops, the group helped design an intervention and establish the collaborative culture needed to support it.
In the first workshop, participants worked in mixed groups to turn raw data into practical information. They sketched layouts and shared ideas, creating visuals of the data that busy staff could understand and use. Based on this view of the data, they agreed on joint decisions staff could make to support families and children earlier.
In the second workshop, participants focused on how partners in Manchester could work together using the data. They explored barriers to joint working across services and set out how they want to collaborate in the future.

heading: What this phase is about
headingPath: What this phase is about
text: In this phase, you test your ideas in a structured way and use the learnings to decide whether and how to iterate. Testing helps you learn quickly and make better decisions about how to reach an outcome.

heading: Main aims of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Main aims of this phase
text:
The main aims of this phase are to:
develop a test plan
test your idea
gather evidence you can learn from
use evidence, assumptions and your theory of change to guide your decisions
iterate what you’re testing, along with your theory of change, assumptions and decisions
know whether you want to continue testing and iterating, pause, scale or stop
You may develop a monitoring and evaluation framework to record longer-term learning.

heading: Outcomes of this phase
headingPath: What this phase is about > Outcomes of this phase
text:
At the end of this phase you should have:
completed at least one test cycle to understand how your idea works in practice
used your findings to guide decisions on what to do next
updated your theory of change based on evidence

heading: Understanding testing
headingPath: Understanding testing
text:
Testing is a way of collecting evidence to guide decisions that help you reach an outcome.
Testing gives you a structure for learning about an idea.
It involves:
an assumption and related hypothesis, covering what you believe is true and the prediction you want to test
an activity, setting out what you do to test the hypothesis
a way to observe and record results, so you can capture learnings

heading: Good practice when testing
headingPath: Understanding testing > Good practice when testing
text:
When you’re testing ideas, you should:
work as a multidisciplinary team so you benefit from the right skills
focus on assumptions with greater uncertainty or risk
focus on shared, measurable outcomes
build an evidence-based understanding of the test idea
combine different types of evidence to make decisions as you test
use learnings to decide whether to iterate, scale, pause or stop
work in the open

heading: Why you should test
headingPath: Understanding testing > Why you should test
text:
Testing moves a team from abstract ideas to making practical design and delivery decisions. It gives you the information you need to decide what to do next.
Testing helps you:
reduce risk by learning what works before investing more time and money
develop better services using feedback from local people and partners
build enthusiasm by bringing ideas to life
challenge assumptions by seeing how an idea works in practice
Before running a test, invest time as a team in agreeing what you hope to achieve. Only test when you’re clear how the results could change your next steps.

heading: Creating a testing plan
headingPath: Creating a testing plan
text:
Make a plan to give structure and purpose to your activities.
Your plan should include:
the aim of your test
assumptions and hypotheses to check
testing methods you’ll use
measures of success
risks and ethical considerations
decisions you’ll make based on results

heading: Setting your test objectives
headingPath: Creating a testing plan > Setting your test objectives
text:
Test and learn lets you start small and make changes to design and delivery before scaling an intervention.
Starting small means:
testing the simplest working version of an idea so early feedback informs your next steps
focusing on your riskiest assumptions first, so you check what matters most before investing further
Set out what you want to achieve from your test and why the test and learn approach suits your challenge area.

heading: Example: setting objectives
headingPath: Creating a testing plan > Setting your test objectives > Example: setting objectives
text:
The Test, Learn and Grow (TLG) team worked with Liverpool City Council and other partners to plan a test for a community healthcare intervention. The aim of the test plan was to prevent and reduce respiratory illness in children aged 5 and under.
The plan identified 3 objectives, to:
see if an intervention used elsewhere in the region could work in Liverpool
check if the intervention could be adapted to the health needs of a new location
find ways to fund and maintain the intervention beyond the test period

heading: Agreeing decision criteria
headingPath: Creating a testing plan > Agreeing decision criteria
text:
List the decisions you need to make and when you need to make them, using your theory of change as a guide.
This list will help you:
choose your testing method
collect the right evidence
involve the right people
Set your decision criteria early so you know how to act on findings. Review your progress regularly and adapt your plan as you gather evidence.
Decide as a team what evidence you need to:
continue or scale – when an idea works and is ready for developing or a larger test
iterate – when an idea shows promise, but needs changes before you test again
pause – when you need more evidence, capacity or a change in conditions before deciding
stop – when evidence shows the idea is not working
Setting criteria at the start protects against 2 common biases:
giving early positive signals more weight than mixed or negative ones
continuing an approach because you put time and effort into it
Make sure the evidence you plan to collect matches the size of the decision.

heading: Identifying assumptions
headingPath: Creating a testing plan > Identifying assumptions
text:
An assumption is something you believe is true, but have not yet proved with evidence.
When developing an idea, you usually make assumptions about:
people’s needs or behaviour, for example “people will use this tool”
feasibility, for example “this idea is technically possible”
impact, for example “earlier conversations will keep people in employment”
List all the assumptions your team is making.

heading: Prioritising assumptions
headingPath: Creating a testing plan > Prioritising assumptions
text:
Focus your testing on your riskiest assumptions. These are the ones that have the biggest impact on your outcomes and the least evidence to support them. You can test the rest later.
To prioritise your riskiest assumptions, you can:
plot them on a grid showing certainty and impact
score them against your decision criteria
Read guidance on prioritising assumptions based on evidence and impact in Chapter 5 of the Magenta Book Test and Learn Annex.

heading: Example: prioritising the riskiest assumption
headingPath: Creating a testing plan > Prioritising assumptions > Example: prioritising the riskiest assumption
text:
In Liverpool, the TLG team worked on a test plan to see whether pop-up clinics and service referrals would improve the respiratory health of children and young people.
They used the riskiest assumptions in their theory of change to design the test. For example, the team identified an assumption that referring families to one service with a high impact on health, like housing support, would be more effective than offering several services.
This assumption was considered to be:
high impact – it affected whether the intervention succeeded
low certainty – there was little evidence to prove or disprove it
To test the assumption, the plan focused on offering referrals across multiple services.

heading: Turning assumptions into hypotheses to test
headingPath: Creating a testing plan > Turning assumptions into hypotheses to test
text:
A hypothesis takes your riskiest assumption and turns it into a prediction you can test.
Writing hypotheses down helps your team agree on what to test, which is an approach known as hypothesis-driven design.
One way to write a hypothesis is:
If we… [do something]
Then… [this will happen]
Because… [reason based on your theory of change or existing evidence]
The change you predict can be short term or long term.

heading: Planning how to test
headingPath: Planning how to test
text:
You should build your test plan on the decisions you need to make. It will define:
your testing methods
the evidence you need
who you test with

heading: Collecting the right amount of evidence
headingPath: Planning how to test > Collecting the right amount of evidence
text:
The evidence you need changes as your service or intervention develops. What counts as ‘good enough’ depends on your context and testing stage. Some decisions need greater certainty and evidence of outcomes. Agree as a team on the type and amount of evidence you need for the stage you’re at.
In early stage testing, your goal is to reduce uncertainty and risk around design decisions. You need less evidence at this stage because the cost of being wrong is low. You have not committed resources or scaled. Look for early signs of impact, including the possibility that your idea might make things worse.
In later stage testing, you need stronger evidence to support decisions that have a big impact on people’s lives.
This evidence helps you decide whether to:
scale an existing service in an area
expand to new places
invest further in an intervention
Read guidance on testing tools, methods and trial design in Chapter 6 of the Magenta Book Test and Learn Annex.

heading: Choosing a testing method
headingPath: Planning how to test > Choosing a testing method
text:
Match your method to what you need to learn.
If you’re exploring ideas and do not yet have a prototype to test, read about using participatory methods for design.
If you have an idea and want to test your assumptions about it, use qualitative interviews, short surveys or user journey mapping.
To learn what works as you build your service or intervention, you can use:
testing with users
qualitative sprints
A/B testing
randomised controlled trials

heading: Example: planning test methods
headingPath: Planning how to test > Choosing a testing method > Example: planning test methods
text:
In Liverpool, the Test, Learn and Grow test plan focused on adapting a successful local health intervention to a new location.
The plan included activities that would quickly find out which:
families the test should focus on in the new location
local support services would most benefit families in the area
These activities involved:
analysis of existing health data to identify relevant families in one neighbourhood
co-design workshops with staff and service users to prototype and iterate the initial service offer

heading: Deciding who to test with
headingPath: Planning how to test > Deciding who to test with
text:
You should test with:
people affected by or using your intervention
practitioners who will deliver it
In early testing you can learn a lot from a small number of well-chosen people. If you’re using qualitative methods, the Service Manual recommends 4 to 8 participants for each round of research.
For quantitative methods, aim for a sample of at least 30 people. Make sure your sample reflects the people the intervention is designed for, matching characteristics such as age or gender.
When you’re evaluating your service, testing with representative participants will give you stronger evidence of impact.
Read the Service Manual guidance on:
planning user research for your service
finding participants for user research

heading: Planning a comparison group
headingPath: Planning how to test > Planning a comparison group
text:
Later in the process, you may need evidence that your intervention caused a specific change.
To measure impact, do not include all eligible users in early testing or delivery.
Plan early who you’ll test with, so you can form a comparison group. You can then measure differences in outcomes between those who have used the intervention and those who have not.

heading: Planning how you will learn
headingPath: Planning how you will learn
text:
Testing is only useful if you use what you learn. Plan your learning before you start testing. Think about:
your measures of success
how you’ll capture data during testing
how your team will review findings
what decisions you need to make based on learnings
Your test idea might not have the effect you want – this is still useful learning.

heading: Defining measures of success
headingPath: Planning how you will learn > Defining measures of success
text:
Decide how you’ll measure success before you start testing. What you measure may change as you learn more.
Your measures should help you understand the impact of an idea or whether your assumptions are correct. Writing hypotheses makes it easier to choose what to track.
Good measures will:
show whether something has happened
help you decide what to do next
Measures are not pass or fail scores. Tracking them consistently over time creates the data need for evaluation.
Read about developing a monitoring and evaluation framework.
Once you’ve chosen your measures, set out how you’ll collect data to track them. Agree as a team on the level and type of evidence you need at each stage of testing. Combining qualitative and quantitative evidence helps you understand how well an test idea works.
Read about collecting the right amount of evidence.

heading: Example: measuring success
headingPath: Planning how you will learn > Defining measures of success > Example: measuring success
text:
In Liverpool, the Test, Learn and Grow team’s test plan aimed to reduce repeat visits to A&E and GPs for respiratory problems by introducing regular clinic appointments.
A short initial test would be unlikely to show changes in these top-level numbers.
Instead the team’s evaluation plan focused on early signs that symptoms were improving and services were dealing with the underlying causes of the illness. For example, the plan set out to measure whether:
people needed less emergency medication after visiting the clinic
children and caregivers took up referrals to support services

heading: Establishing learning routines
headingPath: Planning how you will learn > Establishing learning routines
text:
Agree how your team will learn from the data you collect and insights you generate. You could agree:
the way you document what you learn, such as a learning log
regular routines, such as synthesis sessions to review findings as a team

heading: Managing risks and ethical considerations
headingPath: Planning how you will learn > Managing risks and ethical considerations
text:
Test in a way that is safe, respectful and responsible. Consider and document:
potential risks to participants and team members
ethical practice and how testing will meet standards
data protection
safeguarding, if you test sensitive topics or work with people in vulnerable situations
steps to reduce any risks you identify
Read the guidance on conducting research safely.

heading: Agreeing on your approach with partners and your team
headingPath: Planning how you will learn > Agreeing on your approach with partners and your team
text:
Testing plans can become complex, particularly for methods such as randomised controlled trials. Include evaluation advice in your project to identify complex methods that need extra planning.
Agree testing decisions with your team and partners before writing a detailed plan. For example, you could share a summary that covers:
what you want to learn
how you plan to test
what you’ll measure
the decisions you hope to make
You could also run a workshop with decision makers to agree your approach.

heading: Iterating your solution and testing approach
headingPath: Iterating your solution and testing approach
text:
Use different ways to collect evidence and see how your intervention works for users, so you can make decisions with confidence.
Check new findings by combining them with existing evidence. Comparing evidence is especially important later in testing, when you need confidence to make big decisions.
Read the guidance about combining different types of evidence.
You do not need to wait for later evaluation to collect data. Running small-scale surveys can strengthen your early testing.
To get the most from your evidence:
find out what quantitative data the service already holds, including administrative data, and make sure you have the right data protection documents to use it
plan how you’ll collect new evidence to avoid asking the same people to participate again
map your findings in a team session to see what each test showed and how they fit together
review evidence as a team to agree on findings and next steps
Read the guidance on collecting the right amount of evidence.

heading: Continuous learning and evaluation
headingPath: Continuous learning and evaluation
text:
Record your findings and review what you learn. Use what you learn to inform your next steps. A learning framework helps you keep your wider context in mind alongside day-to-day, small-scale testing. Use it to map evidence against your:
theory of change
assumptions and hypotheses
decisions
You should also keep a change log to record big decisions and changes.

heading: Iterating your theory of change
headingPath: Continuous learning and evaluation > Iterating your theory of change
text:
Update your theory of change as you test if:
new evidence confirms or challenges your assumptions
your activities, resources or outputs change – for example, if you improve a service and need to reflect how you deliver it
your intended outcomes change, which may require a new theory of change
Review your theory of change regularly during planning cycles to:
record what has changed after testing
check that the link between your activities and outcomes still makes sense

heading: Building evaluation into your work
headingPath: Continuous learning and evaluation > Building evaluation into your work
text:
In test and learn, evaluation is not separate from testing. It’s a structured way to measure changes in:
impact
process
implementation
value for money
Base your evaluation on data that tracks how your activities lead to outcomes.
Before you start testing, decide how and when users will receive the intervention. Making delivery plans early ensures you have the right data to prove your impact later, for example by setting up a comparison group. Read about deciding who to test with.
As you move from testing ideas to proving what works, you’ll need stronger evaluation and evidence to show your intervention caused a change. Read about defining measures of success.

heading: Developing a monitoring and evaluation framework
headingPath: Continuous learning and evaluation > Developing a monitoring and evaluation framework
text:
Work with evaluation colleagues to create your monitoring and evaluation framework, using your theory of change as the starting point. The framework helps you:
identify the outputs and outcomes you want to track
write hypotheses to test across the project
Decide how you’ll collect data on your main outcomes from the start. Track this data throughout testing, using:
direct measures – to get the exact information you need
substitute measures – to get related information
your agreed measures of success – to check if you’ve met your overall goals
Continue evaluation once the intervention is set up. This will help you decide whether to scale, iterate, pause or stop. Agree your decision criteria early to make this process easier.

heading: Establishing a culture of test and learn
headingPath: Establishing a culture of test and learn
text: To support test and learn projects, look at how you can influence wider ways of working across your organisation and system.

heading: Setting the right culture
headingPath: Establishing a culture of test and learn > Setting the right culture
text:
Your organisation needs to be willing to take risks on new approaches. Work with leaders to shape a culture that:
tests new ideas, prizes curiosity and accepts failure
encourages shared learning by making it standard practice to work in the open and talk about what does not work, as well as what does work
values collaboration and respects people from different disciplines and backgrounds
supports team wellbeing, recognising that doing things differently requires resilience and strong networks

heading: Sharing what works and what does not
headingPath: Establishing a culture of test and learn > Sharing what works and what does not
text:
Join networks to share your experiences and learn from others. If a network does not exist in your area or sector, consider working with peers to set one up. For example, the South West Test and Learn Network first met in June 2026. Generating interest in test and learn across your organisation and area can help change mindset and culture.
You can also join the national Test, Learn and Grow (TLG) Network to broaden learning and sharing.

heading: Telling stories about your work
headingPath: Establishing a culture of test and learn > Telling stories about your work
text:
Share stories that show the impact of your service or intervention on the people who use it. Storytelling motivates others, and enables them to see why the test and learn approach works.
You can share stories in different ways, for example by:
writing blog posts – see Camden Council’s Change by Design blog for examples
making videos
giving presentations – read the Doing presentations guide by Giles Turnbull
bringing your work to the TLG Network to get community feedback, or starting your own group

heading: Building capabilities
headingPath: Establishing a culture of test and learn > Building capabilities
text:
A range of skills are needed to run test and learn projects, including design, evaluation and research.
You can build these skills by:
setting up dedicated test and learn teams
updating training and leadership programmes to grow local expertise
You’ll also need to work with wider teams so they accept these new ways of working and value input from different disciplines and voices.
Read the guidance on the skills you need in your team.

heading: Giving teams autonomy to make decisions
headingPath: Establishing a culture of test and learn > Giving teams autonomy to make decisions
text: Budget spend can often cause friction. Consider releasing the budget in stages, based on the team meeting agreed outcomes. Delegating financial authority lets teams iterate quickly without having to get approval for every change in direction.

heading: Overcoming barriers to growing test and learn
headingPath: Overcoming barriers to growing test and learn
text:
System barriers can get in the way of teams following a test and learn approach. These barriers range from fragmented funding and complex spending approvals to data sharing and skill gaps.
The Test, Learn and Grow programme is working to solve these issues in central government.
You can also influence conditions in your organisation. For example, leaders can:
change the way internal processes are managed, such as recruitment
create a culture where working in the open is standard practice
work more collaboratively with partners

heading: Example: improved data sharing leads to better decisions
headingPath: Overcoming barriers to growing test and learn > Example: improved data sharing leads to better decisions
text:
Staff in Somerset Council faced a safeguarding challenge because information about children and families was stored in separate systems. As a result, services often missed opportunities to intervene, and families had to retell their story to many different people.
To solve this challenge, a test and learn team created the Transform Family View system. It brings together information from more than 30 data sources across children’s social care, education and health.
The system presents this data in one secure place to show:
a child’s vulnerabilities
which services are involved
who else is supporting the family
actions staff have already taken
Having this information in one place helps staff make better decisions and provide more coordinated support for children.

heading: (untitled)
headingPath: (untitled)
text:
We’ll update this guidance to reflect learning from the Test, Learn and Grow programme and the wider community. Updates will include adding new sections, such as on scaling and sustaining test and learn projects.
You can track changes to this playbook as we make them.
You can also help, by telling us if:
you have a suggestion for new content that would help you adopt test and learn
something is unclear, missing or out of date
the guidance does not work in your organisation
you have an example of good practice we could include
you have used the playbook and are willing to talk to us about the experience
Email the team at tlg-playbook@cabinetoffice.gov.uk.

heading: Previous editions of the Green Book
headingPath: Previous editions of the Green Book
